stemMd:
**Text 1**

Many historians describe the open-field villages of medieval Thornmere as places of fixed custom, where each household farmed the same scattered strips of land that its ancestors had farmed. The village surveys appear to confirm this picture: in survey after survey, the same family names are listed beside the same strips for generations.

**Text 2**

Historian Agathe Duval has found that each Thornmere survey was largely copied from the one before it, often without anyone checking who was actually working the land. Comparing the surveys with village court records of land sales and leases, she found that many strips changed hands several times in a single decade, even while the surveys went on listing the same families.

Based on the texts, how would Duval (Text 2) most likely respond to the evidence described in Text 1?

options.label: A
options.textMd: She would agree that it shows that strips of land in Thornmere rarely changed hands.

options.label: B
options.textMd: She would argue that it reflects how the surveys were made rather than who held the land.

options.label: C
options.textMd: She would argue that it is accurate for the largest households but not for smaller ones.

options.label: D
options.textMd: She would argue that it is accurate, but only for the years before the village courts began keeping records.

explanationMd:
Start by pinning down the evidence in Text 1: the same family names appear beside the same strips in survey after survey. Historians read that as proof that land stayed in the same families.

Text 2 explains where that repetition came from. Each survey was copied from the previous one without checking, so names would repeat whether or not the land had changed hands, and court records show it often had. Duval would therefore say the repeated names are a product of the copying, not a record of who held the land. That is the choice saying the evidence reflects how the surveys were made rather than who held the land.

A useful check in cross-text items is to ask whether the second author accepts the first author's evidence at face value. Duval does not: she explains it away. Any choice in which she agrees with it, or accepts it in part on grounds the text never mentions, can be eliminated.

distractorRationale.a: Duval's court-record evidence shows many strips changing hands several times in a decade, so she would reject the conclusion that land rarely changed hands.
distractorRationale.c: Text 2 never distinguishes between large and small households. Duval's objection applies to the surveys as a whole, because every survey was copied from the one before.
distractorRationale.d: Text 2 never mentions a period before the courts kept records. Duval's objection is that every survey was copied from the one before without checking, a flaw that would affect the surveys in any period, so she gives no reason to trust them for some years and not others.

accessibilityText: Two short history texts. Text 1: many historians describe the open-field villages of medieval Thornmere as places of fixed custom, where each household farmed the same scattered strips its ancestors had farmed; the village surveys appear to confirm this, listing the same family names beside the same strips for generations. Text 2: historian Agathe Duval has found that each Thornmere survey was largely copied from the one before, often without checking who was actually working the land; comparing the surveys with village court records of land sales and leases, she found many strips changed hands several times in a single decade, even while the surveys kept listing the same families. The question asks how Duval would most likely respond to the evidence in Text 1. The choices are: she would agree that it shows strips rarely changed hands; she would argue that it reflects how the surveys were made rather than who held the land; she would argue that it is accurate for the largest households but not smaller ones; and she would argue that it is accurate, but only for the years before the village courts began keeping records.

provenance.notes: Original cross-text item. Thornmere, its surveys and Duval's findings are invented. Text 2 explains away the evidence that Text 1 relies on.

review.author: sat-wave8-rw-author

independentSolve.workingNotes: Duval shows surveys were copied from earlier ones, so repeated family names reflect copying practice, not actual landholding. Agreeing that strips rarely changed hands contradicts her court-record findings; large vs. small households and pre-court-record years are never discussed. [A second, separate blind solve (blind-reviewer-wave8-sat-rw-run1) reached the same answer: Duval found the surveys were copied forward without checking, while court records show frequent transfers, so the repeated names reflect survey-making practice, not landholding. She would not agree strips rarely changed hands; household size and pre-court-record periods are never discussed.]

review.notes: Options were reordered after review to remove answer-position bias; ids and labels were remapped with the key.
